content: A five-kilometer section of the United States border fence stretches between the Otay Mesa Border Crossing in San Diego, California, and the Pacific Ocean. This structure, often referred to as the San Diego wall, was completed in the early 1990s. While there are other border walls at various points along the U.S.-Mexico border, the Tortilla Wall is currently the longest. The Tortilla Wall is adorned with graffiti, crosses, photographs, and memorials dedicated to individuals who have lost their lives attempting to cross into the United States illegally. Following the construction of a security fence in the region, apprehensions of individuals attempting to cross the border dropped significantly, from 202,000 in 1992 to 9,000 in 1994. The construction of the Tortilla Wall is widely perceived by many Mexicans as an unfriendly gesture. It has become a symbol of the contentious immigration debate. Critics argue that the wall does not prevent illegal crossings but instead redirects them to more perilous areas, such as the Arizona desert. The U.S. government has allocated $2 billion to construct an additional 700 miles (approximately 1,100 kilometers) of fencing along the southern border with Mexico. Despite the wall, tunnels remain a common method for crossing the border. Some of these tunnels are highly sophisticated. For example, one tunnel built by smugglers extended half a mile from Tijuana to San Diego, featuring a concrete floor and electrical wiring. Other tunnels have included steel rails, while some are rudimentary dirt passageways or are connected to sewer or drainage systems.
